summary: Contains the text of the agreement between ISOC and the IETF on one side and ISO/IEC JTC1/SC6 on the other, covering cooperative development of the IS-IS routing protocol. It defines the scope of each group's work, asks IANA to maintain an IS-IS registry, and sets collaboration guidelines. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IS-IS is maintained by ISO/IEC while the IETF develops Internet-related extensions. RFC 3563 records how the two organizations divide work and keep each other informed.

subtitle: An agreement that divides IS-IS routing development between the IETF and ISO/IEC JTC1/SC6.

tldr.problem: The IETF and ISO/IEC JTC1/SC6 both work on IS-IS, so they needed a process for assigning work and avoiding changes that conflict.
tldr.mechanism: The agreement distinguishes the core IS-IS mechanisms from Internet-specific extensions, assigns each organization's scope, and describes registry and review procedures.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3563 records a process agreement rather than a protocol. It has been updated by RFC 6233.

today: RFC 3563 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 6233. It records a process agreement, not a protocol.

sections.title: Why the Organizations Made an Agreement
sections.content:
RFC 3563 contains an annex to a cooperative agreement between the Internet Society and IETF, on one side, and ISO/IEC JTC1/SC6, on the other. The agreement concerns development of the IS-IS intra-domain routing protocol, specified as ISO/IEC 10589.

JTC1/SC6 maintains the IS-IS standard. The IETF IS-IS Working Group develops extensions for use within the Internet. The annex records a process for coordinating this work.
sections.plainLanguage: Two standards groups work on IS-IS. This agreement explains how they coordinate so each group knows which changes it is responsible for.

sections.title: Core IS-IS and Internet-Specific Extensions
sections.content:
The agreement defines the core IS-IS mechanisms as the protocol elements specified in ISO/IEC 10589. These include the packet framework, encapsulation, adjacency formation, designated intermediate system election, link-state packet synchronization and flooding, database maintenance, and topology model.

Internet-specific extensions fall within the IETF's work scope. An extension can qualify when it does not change the core in a way that affects non-IP implementations, adds supplementary mechanisms not generally relevant to non-IP implementations, or records a de facto implementation agreement that is not generally applicable to them. New TLVs that do not alter core algorithms in a way that harms interoperability are not considered a core modification.
sections.plainLanguage: JTC1/SC6 maintains the core protocol. The IETF can develop Internet-focused additions when they do not break the core behavior expected by other IS-IS users.

sections.title: Where Extensions Are Standardized
sections.content:
The agreement says JTC1/SC6 will not standardize Internet-specific extensions, while the IETF may do so under its own standards process. Extensions developed by the IETF that need standardization but are not Internet-specific should be submitted to JTC1/SC6. The IETF will publish those as Informational RFCs rather than standards-track RFCs.

IETF submissions to JTC1 use its fast-track procedure, while the IETF applies its Proposed Standard procedures to review the work. Standards-track IS-IS documents must explain why the extension is Internet-specific. Unclear cases are decided through discussion between representatives of the two organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet-only additions may be standardized through the IETF. Other changes should go to JTC1/SC6, with review steps agreed by both organizations.

sections.title: The IS-IS TLV Registry
sections.content:
Until JTC1/SC6 provides a registry service, the agreement asks IANA to maintain a registry for IS-IS TLV codepoints. The values range from 0 to 255, and allocations require approval by an IESG-designated expert.

The IETF will keep JTC1/SC6 informed about allocated values, and JTC1/SC6 will direct allocation requests to the IANA process. When JTC1/SC6 can take over registry management, authority transfers to it; IANA may retain the registry for information.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the numbered list of IS-IS TLV values for now. The agreement describes how requests are reviewed and how the list can later move to JTC1/SC6.

sections.title: Communication and Document Review
sections.content:
The IETF and JTC1/SC6 agree to inform each other about new IS-IS work. They may communicate directly or use liaison representatives. Members of JTC1/SC6 may review IETF documents and send comments to the working group or its leadership.

JTC1/SC6 is encouraged to request IETF review of its IS-IS work by sharing it as an informational Internet-Draft. The RFC says this kind of non-protocol document does not directly affect Internet security.
sections.plainLanguage: Each organization promises to share news about new work and give the other a chance to review relevant drafts.
